summary: Defines the protocol used between an IRC client and server, assuming the reader knows the IRC architecture. It covers how users connect, send messages and issue commands. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2812 defines how an Internet Relay Chat (IRC) client sends commands to a server and reads the server's replies. It covers connecting, choosing a nickname, joining channels, sending messages and asking for network information.

subtitle: The text commands and replies used between an IRC client and server.

tldr.problem: An IRC client needs a defined message format and commands to register, join channels, send text and query an IRC server.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol uses text lines with an optional prefix, command and parameters. It specifies registration, channel operations, messaging, server queries, optional commands and numeric replies.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2812 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459 and focuses on compatibility with existing clients. It notes that IRC software version 2.10 was the only complete implementation at publication.

today: RFC 2812 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 2812.

sections.title: Client, User and Channel Names
sections.content:
This memo defines the client-to-server protocol for IRC and assumes familiarity with the IRC architecture in RFC 2810. A server is named with a string of up to 63 characters. Users have nicknames of up to 9 characters, and services are named using a nickname and server name.

Channel names begin with &, number sign, + or !, may be up to 50 characters and are case-insensitive. The meaning of these channel types is described in RFC 2811, not in the client protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients, users, services and channels each have identifiers. The channel prefix indicates which channel type a name refers to.

sections.title: Message Format and Replies
sections.content:
An IRC message contains an optional prefix, a command and up to 15 parameters, separated by spaces. A prefix begins with a colon and identifies the message origin. Commands are words or three-digit numbers. Messages end with CR-LF and cannot exceed 512 characters including that ending, leaving 510 characters for the command and parameters.

Servers often answer with a numeric reply used for either a normal result or an error. Wildcard masks use question mark to match one character and asterisk to match any number of characters; a backslash can escape either wildcard.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command is one line with a sender, an instruction and any details. The line has a length limit, and the server answers with a message that often starts with a numeric code.

sections.title: Registering a Connection
sections.content:
A client registers as a user with NICK and USER, or as a service with SERVICE. A connection password is optional, but PASS must be sent before the registration command that completes the connection. The recommended user sequence is PASS, NICK and USER.

After successful user registration, the server sends RPL_WELCOME; a service receives RPL_YOURESERVICE. The client can later use QUIT to end its session. OPER requests operator privileges using a name and password.
sections.plainLanguage: A user gives the server a nickname and user details to register. If the connection uses a password, the client sends it before completing registration.

sections.title: Channels and Text Messages
sections.content:
JOIN asks to join a channel; the special argument 0 asks to leave all current channels. After a successful join, the server sends the channel topic and member list. Other channel commands include PART, MODE, TOPIC, NAMES, LIST, INVITE and KICK.

PRIVMSG sends text to a user or channel. NOTICE is similar, but automatic replies must never be sent in response to it; this avoids loops between clients that automatically answer messages. SQUERY sends text to a service.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks to join a channel before receiving its messages. It can send text to another user or channel, and NOTICE must not trigger automatic replies.

sections.title: Queries, Optional Features and Status
sections.content:
Clients can query servers for information such as message of the day, network size, version, statistics, links, time, administration and server details. WHO, WHOIS and WHOWAS request information about users. PING and PONG check whether the other end of a connection is responding.

The RFC also lists optional commands, including AWAY, REHASH, DIE, RESTART, SUMMON and ISON. Its current-problems section notes that nickname collisions can prevent registration or cause both users to be removed. It refers readers to RFC 2813 for security considerations, which are mainly server-side.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can ask the server about its network, users and operating state. The memo also lists optional commands and notes that limited nickname choices can lead to collisions.
